'''Rose Rand''' (born '''Rozalia Rand''', {{IPA|de-AT|rand|lang}}; June 14, 1903 – July 28, 1980) was an Austrian-American [[logician]] and [[philosopher]]. She was a member of the [[Vienna Circle]].

== Life and work ==

Rose (Rozalia) Rand was born in [[Lemberg]] in the Austrian crown land of [[Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria|Galicia]] (today, Lviv, [[Ukraine]]).<ref name="The Vienna Circle and Its Periphery">{{cite book |last=Stadler |first=Friedrich |chapter=The Vienna Circle and Its Periphery: Biographies and Biobibliographies |date=2015 |title=The Vienna Circle: Studies in the Origins, Development, and Influence of Logical Empiricism |volume=4 |pages=397–596 |editor-last=Stadler |editor-first=Friedrich |series=Vienna Circle Institute Library |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-16561-5_12 |isbn=9783319165615 }}</ref><ref name="History of Women Philosophers">{{Cite web|url=https://historyofwomenphilosophers.org/project/directory-of-women-philosophers/rose-rand/|title=Rose Rand - History of Women Philosophers and Scientists|access-date=2019-06-13}}</ref> After her family had moved to [[Austria]] she studied at the Polish [[Gymnasium (school)|Gymnasium]] in [[Vienna]].<ref name="The Vienna Circle and Its Periphery" /> In 1924 she enrolled in [[Vienna University]], her teachers included [[Heinrich Gomperz]], [[Moritz Schlick]], and [[Rudolf Carnap]].<ref name="Guide to papers" /> She graduated with her first degree in 1928.<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /> During her post-graduation years, she  remained in contact with Vienna Circle colleagues such as Schlick.<ref name="Guide to papers">{{cite web|url=https://digital.library.pitt.edu/islandora/object/pitt%3AUS-PPiU-asp199001/viewer|title=Guide to the Rose Rand's Papers 1903-1981|last=Rand|first=Rose|date=|website=|publisher=Special Collections Department, University of Pittsburgh|archive-url=|archive-date=|accessdate=September 19, 2013}}</ref>

As a PhD candidate, Rand participated regularly in the Vienna Circle discussions, and kept records of these discussions, she was most active in the Vienna Circle from 1930 to 1935.<ref name="Guide to papers" /><ref name="geschichte" />  Between 1930 and 1937 she worked, and took part in research, at the Psychiatric-neurological Clinic of Vienna University.<ref name="Woman in Logic" /> She also earned money by tutoring students, giving adult education classes, and translating Polish articles on logic.<ref name="The Vienna Circle and Its Periphery" /><ref name="Woman in Logic">{{cite book |last=Hamacher-Hermes |first=Adelheid |chapter=Rose Rand: a Woman in Logic |date=2003 |title=The Vienna Circle and Logical Empiricism: Re-Evaluation and Future Perspectives |volume=10 |pages=365–378 |editor-last=Stadler |editor-first=Friedrich |series=Vienna Circle Institute Yearbook |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/0-306-48214-2_29 |isbn=9780306482144 }}</ref>

In 1937 her doctoral thesis on [[Tadeusz Kotarbiński]]'s philosophy was approved and she completed her PhD [[Thesis defense|viva]].<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /> In 1938, on the same day she completed her final doctoral exam, she was awarded her PhD.<ref name="Woman in Logic" /> As a [[Jew]], however, she was barred from her profession.<ref name="geschichte">{{Cite web |last=Kniefacz |first=Katharina |date= |title=Rose Rand, Prof. Dr. (14.6.1903 – 28.7.1980) |url=https://geschichte.univie.ac.at/en/persons/rose-rand |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date= |website=website of the University of Vienna}}</ref>

Rose Rand, unemployed and of Jewish descent, suffered great difficulties in pre-[[World War II]] Vienna. In 1939, with the assistance of [[Susan Stebbing]], she finally emigrated to [[London]] as a Jew [[Statelessness|without nationality]].<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" />

After a period of time in England in which she worked as a [[nurse]] she was admitted as "distinguished foreigner" at the faculty of Moral Science at [[Cambridge University]].<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /> There she attended the seminars of [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]].<ref name="Guide to papers" /> In 1943 she lost her privileges and had to work at a metal factory, and teach night classes in [[German language|German]] and [[psychology]] in the Luton Technical College and Tottenham Technical College.<ref name="The Vienna Circle and Its Periphery" /><ref name="geschichte" /> Between 1943 and 1950 she also worked in practical [[engineering]].<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /> [[Karl Popper]] helped her to get a small research grant, so she could attend [[Oxford University]] as a "recognized student" <ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /> from 1950 to 1954.<ref name="Woman in Logic" />

Rand moved to the [[United States]] in 1954. There she sought academic employment and initially attempted to pursue her research at the libraries of [[Princeton University|Princeton]] and [[Harvard University|Harvard]] universities.<ref name="Guide to papers" /> Between 1955 and 1959 she held temporary positions teaching elementary math, ancient philosophy and logic, and was a research associate, in the [[University of Chicago]], [[Indiana University Northwest]] in [[Gary, Indiana|Gary]], and [[Notre Dame University]].<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /><ref name="Guide to papers" />

In 1959 she returned to [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] and after that to [[Princeton, New Jersey]].<ref name="Guide to papers" /> In the following years she earned her living from grants and fellowships which were given to her mostly for her work on translations of Polish and Russian logicians.<ref name="Guide to papers" />  When not supported by grants Rand operated on private loans and other financial assistance, freelance translation work, or sporadic temporary employment.<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /><ref name="Guide to papers" />

Rose Rand died on 28 July 1980 in Princeton, aged 77.<ref name="History of Women Philosophers" /><ref name="Guide to papers" />

Rand's records at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] contain, among other things, her research, the records of the discussions in the Vienna Circle and over 1,600 letters to [[Otto Neurath]], [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]], [[Alfred Tarski]] and others.<ref name="Guide to papers" /> Some of her correspondence (from her time as an ''émigré'' in England) is also held by [[Oxford University]]'s [[Bodleian Library]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Rentetzi |first=Maria |chapter='I Want to Look Like a Lady, Not Like a Factory Worker' Rose Rand, a Woman Philosopher of the Vienna Circle |date=2010 |title=EPSA Epistemology and Methodology of Science: Launch of the European Philosophy of Science Association |pages=233–244 |editor-last=Suárez |editor-first=Mauricio |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en|doi=10.1007/978-90-481-3263-8_20 |isbn=9789048132638 |editor2-last=Dorato |editor2-first=Mauro |editor3-last=Rédei |editor3-first=Miklós}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bodley.ox.ac.uk/dept/scwmss/wmss/online/modern/spsl/spsl.html|title=SPSL Archive|website=www.bodley.ox.ac.uk|access-date=2019-06-14}}</ref>
